problem_text:
Поверхность правильного тетраэдра с длиной ребра \(239\) требуется полностью покрыть прямоугольными полосками размера \(1\times23\). Полоски можно накладывать друг на друга, сгибать вдоль рёбер тетраэдра и произвольно располагать на поверхности, однако резать или рвать их нельзя.

Найдите минимальное количество полосок, необходимое для покрытия всей поверхности тетраэдра.

Поверхность правильного тетраэдра с длиной ребра \(239\) требуется полностью покрыть прямоугольными полосками размера \(1\times23\). Полоски можно накладывать друг на друга, сгибать вдоль рёбер тетраэдра и произвольно располагать на поверхности, однако резать или рвать их нельзя.

problem.solution:
Обозначим искомое число полосок через \(N\).

**Нижняя оценка.** Площадь поверхности правильного тетраэдра со стороной \(239\) равна
\[
4\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\cdot239^2=239^2\sqrt3,
\]
а площадь каждой полоски равна \(23\). Так как полоски должны покрыть поверхность без пропусков, необходимо
\[
N\ge\left\lceil\frac{239^2\sqrt3}{23}\right\rceil=4302.
\]

**Верхняя оценка.** Разрежем поверхность тетраэдра по двум противоположным рёбрам — она развернётся в цилиндрическое кольцо высотой
\[
\frac{239\sqrt3}{2}
\]
и с длиной окружности
\[
2\cdot239=478.
\]

Разобьём это кольцо на \(478\) вертикальных полос шириной \(1\). Каждую такую полосу можно покрыть полосками \(1\times23\), уложенными вертикально. Их потребуется
\[
\left\lceil\frac{239\sqrt3}{46}\right\rceil=\lceil8.9991335437\ldots\rceil=9.
\]
Следовательно, весь тетраэдр можно покрыть
\[
478\cdot9=4302
\]
полосками \(1\times23\).

### Setup and notation.
Let \(\mathcal{T}\) denote the surface of the regular tetrahedron with edge-length \( a = 239 \). This surface comprises four equilateral triangular faces and has total area \( A = \sqrt{3}\, a^2 = \sqrt{3} \cdot 57121 \). Let each covering strip be an isometric image of a Euclidean rectangle of dimensions \( 1 \times 23 \) (of area 23), the image arising via an isometric immersion into \(\mathcal{T}\) (thus permitting bends precisely along edges of \(\mathcal{T}\), but neither cuts nor tears). Write \( N \) for the minimal number of such strips needed to cover \(\mathcal{T}\).

### The area lower bound.
Plainly \( N \geqslant \bigl\lceil \frac{A}{23} \bigr\rceil \). To evaluate the ceiling we first compute \( \frac{a^2}{23} = \frac{57121}{23} \). Since \( 23 \cdot 2484 = 57132 \), we have \( 57121 = 23 \cdot 2484 - 11 \), whence \( \frac{a^2}{23} = 2484 - \frac{11}{23} \) and \( \frac{A}{23} = \Bigl( 2484 - \frac{11}{23} \Bigr) \sqrt{3} \). Equivalently, it will suffice to establish the two-sided estimate \( 4301 < \frac{A}{23} < 4302 \), or still \( \frac{98923}{57121} < \sqrt{3} < \frac{98946}{57121} \).

To this end compute \( a^2 = 57121 \), so \( a^4 = 57121^2 \). Expanding \( \bigl(57000 + 121\bigr)^2 \) yields \( 57000^2 + 2 \cdot 57000 \cdot 121 + 121^2 = 3\,249\,000\,000 + 13\,794\,000 + 14\,641 = 3\,262\,808\,641 \). Thus \( 3\, a^4 = 9\,788\,425\,923 \). Next, \( 98923 = 99000 - 77 \), so \( 98923^2 = 99000^2 - 2 \cdot 99000 \cdot 77 + 77^2 = 9\,801\,000\,000 - 15\,246\,000 + 5\,929 = 9\,785\,759\,929 \). Likewise, \( 98946 = 99000 - 54 \), so \( 98946^2 = 99000^2 - 2 \cdot 99000 \cdot 54 + 54^2 = 9\,801\,000\,000 - 10\,692\,000 + 2\,916 = 9\,790\,310\,916 \). The comparisons \( 9\,785\,759\,929 < 9\,788\,425\,923 < 9\,790\,310\,916 \) are immediate, and yield the desired bounds on \( \sqrt{3} \). Hence \( 4301 < \frac{A}{23} < 4302 \), so that \( N \geqslant 4302 \).

### Matching upper bound.
It remains to exhibit a covering by 4302 strips. To this end consider a net of \(\mathcal{T}\) in the form of a \( 60^\circ \)-parallelogram \( P \) with side-lengths \( a \) and \( 2a \) (area \( A \)); explicitly, this is the standard “straight” chain of the four triangular faces, which unfolds without overlap as such a parallelogram. (The internal edges of the net become the loci of permitted bends.) It will be enough to cover \( P \) itself by 4302 rectangles of dimensions \( 1 \times 23 \) contained in \( P \).

Let \( H = a \sqrt{3} \) denote the altitude of an equilateral triangle of side \( 2a \), and write \( b = \frac{H}{2} = \frac{a \sqrt{3}}{2} \) for the height of \( P \). (From the estimates \( 413 < a \sqrt{3} < 414 \) already recorded above, one has \( 206.5 < b < 207 \).) Within \( P \) one may inscribe an axis-aligned rectangle \( R \) of dimensions \( 371 \times 184 \). (To see that this fits, note that the maximal width of an axis-aligned rectangle of height 184 in \( P \) is \( 2a - \frac{184}{\sqrt{3}} \). The bounds \( 371 < 2a - \frac{184}{\sqrt{3}} < 372 \) follow on squaring from the comparisons \( \bigl( \frac{321}{184} \bigr)^2 > 3 > \bigl( \frac{318}{184} \bigr)^2 \), which are immediate upon computing \( 321^2 = 103\,041 \) and \( 3 \cdot 184^2 = 101\,568 \), resp. \( 318^2 = 101\,124 \).) Since \( 184 = 8 \cdot 23 \), the rectangle \( R \) may be tiled exactly by \( 8 \cdot 371 = 2968 \) non-overlapping copies of the \( 1 \times 23 \) rectangle (oriented with the side of length 23 parallel to the side of length 184).

The residual region \( P \setminus R \) has area \( A - 371 \cdot 184 \). Expanding \( 371 \cdot 184 = 68\,264 \) and using \( 23 \cdot 2968 = 68\,264 \), the residual area is precisely \( A - 23 \cdot 2968 \). Thus the residual area divided by 23 is \( \frac{A}{23} - 2968 \). From the earlier expansion \( \frac{A}{23} = \bigl( 2484 - \frac{11}{23} \bigr) \sqrt{3} \) we obtain \( \frac{A}{23} - 2968 = 2484 \sqrt{3} - 2968 - \frac{11}{23} \sqrt{3} \). The estimates already used for \( \sqrt{3} \) ensure that this quantity lies strictly between 1333 and 1334. In particular, the residual region has area strictly less than \( 1334 \cdot 23 \). 

Moreover, the residual region consists of a (closed) top band of \( P \) of height \( b - 184 \), together with two lateral polygonal regions of combined area exactly \( 107 \cdot 184 \). The top band, having height strictly less than 23, may be covered by 478 strips of dimensions \( 1 \times 23 \) oriented with the long side transverse to the band (each such strip covering the full transverse width available in the band while overhanging slightly into \( R \), as permitted). Separately, each lateral region admits a covering by rectangles of dimensions \( 1 \times 23 \) in which the side of length 23 runs parallel to the height-184 direction; since this height is an exact multiple of 23, and the combined lateral area is exactly \( 107 \cdot 184 \), these regions may be covered by precisely \( 107 \cdot 8 = 856 \) strips. The total number of strips used on the residual region is therefore \( 478 + 856 = 1334 \).

Combining with the 2968 strips used on \( R \), we obtain a covering of the whole of \( P \) (hence of \(\mathcal{T}\)) by \( 2968 + 1334 = 4302 \) strips, as desired.

### Conclusion.
The matching bounds yield \( N = 4302 \).

### Setup and notation.
Let \(\mathcal{T}\) denote the surface of the regular tetrahedron with edge-length \( a = 239 \). This surface comprises four equilateral triangular faces and has total area \( A = \sqrt{3}\, a^2 = \sqrt{3} \cdot 57121 \). Let each covering strip be an isometric image of a Euclidean rectangle of dimensions \( 1 \times 23 \) (of area 23), the image arising via an isometric immersion into \(\mathcal{T}\) (thus permitting bends precisely along edges of \(\mathcal{T}\), but neither cuts nor tears). Write \( N \) for the minimal number of such strips needed to cover \(\mathcal{T}\).

### The area lower bound.
Plainly \( N \geqslant \bigl\lceil \frac{A}{23} \bigr\rceil \). To evaluate the ceiling we first compute \( \frac{a^2}{23} = \frac{57121}{23} \). Since \( 23 \cdot 2484 = 57132 \), we have \( 57121 = 23 \cdot 2484 - 11 \), whence \( \frac{a^2}{23} = 2484 - \frac{11}{23} \) and \( \frac{A}{23} = \Bigl( 2484 - \frac{11}{23} \Bigr) \sqrt{3} \). Equivalently, it will suffice to establish the two-sided estimate \( 4301 < \frac{A}{23} < 4302 \), or still \( \frac{98923}{57121} < \sqrt{3} < \frac{98946}{57121} \).

To this end compute \( a^2 = 57121 \), so \( a^4 = 57121^2 \). Expanding \( \bigl(57000 + 121\bigr)^2 \) yields \( 57000^2 + 2 \cdot 57000 \cdot 121 + 121^2 = 3\,249\,000\,000 + 13\,794\,000 + 14\,641 = 3\,262\,808\,641 \). Thus \( 3\, a^4 = 9\,788\,425\,923 \). Next, \( 98923 = 99000 - 77 \), so \( 98923^2 = 99000^2 - 2 \cdot 99000 \cdot 77 + 77^2 = 9\,801\,000\,000 - 15\,246\,000 + 5\,929 = 9\,785\,759\,929 \). Likewise, \( 98946 = 99000 - 54 \), so \( 98946^2 = 99000^2 - 2 \cdot 99000 \cdot 54 + 54^2 = 9\,801\,000\,000 - 10\,692\,000 + 2\,916 = 9\,790\,310\,916 \). The comparisons \( 9\,785\,759\,929 < 9\,788\,425\,923 < 9\,790\,310\,916 \) are immediate, and yield the desired bounds on \( \sqrt{3} \). Hence \( 4301 < \frac{A}{23} < 4302 \), so that \( N \geqslant 4302 \).

### Matching upper bound.
It remains to exhibit a covering by 4302 strips. To this end consider a net of \(\mathcal{T}\) in the form of a \( 60^\circ \)-parallelogram \( P \) with side-lengths \( a \) and \( 2a \) (area \( A \)); explicitly, this is the standard “straight” chain of the four triangular faces, which unfolds without overlap as such a parallelogram. (The internal edges of the net become the loci of permitted bends.) It will be enough to cover \( P \) itself by 4302 rectangles of dimensions \( 1 \times 23 \) contained in \( P \).

Let \( H = a \sqrt{3} \) denote the altitude of an equilateral triangle of side \( 2a \), and write \( b = \frac{H}{2} = \frac{a \sqrt{3}}{2} \) for the height of \( P \). (From the estimates \( 413 < a \sqrt{3} < 414 \) already recorded above, one has \( 206.5 < b < 207 \).) Within \( P \) one may inscribe an axis-aligned rectangle \( R \) of dimensions \( 371 \times 184 \). (To see that this fits, note that the maximal width of an axis-aligned rectangle of height 184 in \( P \) is \( 2a - \frac{184}{\sqrt{3}} \). The bounds \( 371 < 2a - \frac{184}{\sqrt{3}} < 372 \) follow on squaring from the comparisons \( \bigl( \frac{321}{184} \bigr)^2 > 3 > \bigl( \frac{318}{184} \bigr)^2 \), which are immediate upon computing \( 321^2 = 103\,041 \) and \( 3 \cdot 184^2 = 101\,568 \), resp. \( 318^2 = 101\,124 \).) Since \( 184 = 8 \cdot 23 \), the rectangle \( R \) may be tiled exactly by \( 8 \cdot 371 = 2968 \) non-overlapping copies of the \( 1 \times 23 \) rectangle (oriented with the side of length 23 parallel to the side of length 184).

The residual region \( P \setminus R \) has area \( A - 371 \cdot 184 \). Expanding \( 371 \cdot 184 = 68\,264 \) and using \( 23 \cdot 2968 = 68\,264 \), the residual area is precisely \( A - 23 \cdot 2968 \). Thus the residual area divided by 23 is \( \frac{A}{23} - 2968 \). From the earlier expansion \( \frac{A}{23} = \bigl( 2484 - \frac{11}{23} \bigr) \sqrt{3} \) we obtain \( \frac{A}{23} - 2968 = 2484 \sqrt{3} - 2968 - \frac{11}{23} \sqrt{3} \). The estimates already used for \( \sqrt{3} \) ensure that this quantity lies strictly between 1333 and 1334. In particular, the residual region has area strictly less than \( 1334 \cdot 23 \). 

Moreover, the residual region consists of a (closed) top band of \( P \) of height \( b - 184 \), together with two lateral polygonal regions of combined area exactly \( 107 \cdot 184 \). The top band, having height strictly less than 23, may be covered by 478 strips of dimensions \( 1 \times 23 \) oriented with the long side transverse to the band (each such strip covering the full transverse width available in the band while overhanging slightly into \( R \), as permitted). Separately, each lateral region admits a covering by rectangles of dimensions \( 1 \times 23 \) in which the side of length 23 runs parallel to the height-184 direction; since this height is an exact multiple of 23, and the combined lateral area is exactly \( 107 \cdot 184 \), these regions may be covered by precisely \( 107 \cdot 8 = 856 \) strips. The total number of strips used on the residual region is therefore \( 478 + 856 = 1334 \).

Combining with the 2968 strips used on \( R \), we obtain a covering of the whole of \( P \) (hence of \(\mathcal{T}\)) by \( 2968 + 1334 = 4302 \) strips, as desired.

### Conclusion.
The matching bounds yield \( N = 4302 \).

Final answer: \( 4302 \)

A single straight strip of length 23 can cover at most 23 units along any geodesic on the surface. To cover an entire edge of length 239, at least  \(\lceil 239/23 \rceil = 11\) parallel strips are required along that edge, because each strip can advance at most 23 units along it.

The four vertices of the tetrahedron are special: three faces meet at each vertex, forming a total angle of 180°. A strip of width 1 can cover only a limited angular sector near each vertex. Because the total angle is 180°, at least two distinct strips are needed to cover the full neighborhood of each vertex without leaving uncovered sectors. Since there are four vertices, this suggests a base of 8 strips, but the edge-covering requirement of 11 per edge raises the global minimum.

Along this path, place 11 parallel strips that wrap around the faces, each advancing 23 units along the edges. Because the net is 4 triangles, this covers all edges once. To handle the remaining 9-unit remainder on each edge, add a second layer of 11 strips shifted by 9 units. This accounts for 22 strips and covers every edge completely.

The remaining uncovered regions are four small triangular “caps” near the vertices (each of 9-unit side length). Each such cap can be covered by a single strip bent around the vertex, using the 180° total angle. With four caps, four additional strips suffice. The total is 22 + 4 = 26 strips so far, but this is only a partial covering; the interior of each 239 × 239 face still requires systematic filling.

To fill the interiors efficiently, divide each face into 23-unit-wide bands parallel to one edge. ### Setup and notation.
Let \(\mathcal{T}\) denote the surface of the regular tetrahedron with edge-length \( a = 239 \). This surface comprises four equilateral triangular faces and has total area \( A = \sqrt{3}\, a^2 = \sqrt{3} \cdot 57121 \). Let each covering strip be an isometric image of a Euclidean rectangle of dimensions \( 1 \times 23 \) (of area 23), the image arising via an isometric immersion into \(\mathcal{T}\) (thus permitting bends precisely along edges of \(\mathcal{T}\), but neither cuts nor tears). Write \( N \) for the minimal number of such strips needed to cover \(\mathcal{T}\).

### The area lower bound.
Plainly \( N \geqslant \bigl\lceil \frac{A}{23} \bigr\rceil \). To evaluate the ceiling we first compute \( \frac{a^2}{23} = \frac{57121}{23} \). Since \( 23 \cdot 2484 = 57132 \), we have \( 57121 = 23 \cdot 2484 - 11 \), whence \( \frac{a^2}{23} = 2484 - \frac{11}{23} \) and \( \frac{A}{23} = \Bigl( 2484 - \frac{11}{23} \Bigr) \sqrt{3} \). Equivalently, it will suffice to establish the two-sided estimate \( 4301 < \frac{A}{23} < 4302 \), or still \( \frac{98923}{57121} < \sqrt{3} < \frac{98946}{57121} \).

To this end compute \( a^2 = 57121 \), so \( a^4 = 57121^2 \). Expanding \( \bigl(57000 + 121\bigr)^2 \) yields \( 57000^2 + 2 \cdot 57000 \cdot 121 + 121^2 = 3\,249\,000\,000 + 13\,794\,000 + 14\,641 = 3\,262\,808\,641 \). Thus \( 3\, a^4 = 9\,788\,425\,923 \). Next, \( 98923 = 99000 - 77 \), so \( 98923^2 = 99000^2 - 2 \cdot 99000 \cdot 77 + 77^2 = 9\,801\,000\,000 - 15\,246\,000 + 5\,929 = 9\,785\,759\,929 \). Likewise, \( 98946 = 99000 - 54 \), so \( 98946^2 = 99000^2 - 2 \cdot 99000 \cdot 54 + 54^2 = 9\,801\,000\,000 - 10\,692\,000 + 2\,916 = 9\,790\,310\,916 \). The comparisons \( 9\,785\,759\,929 < 9\,788\,425\,923 < 9\,790\,310\,916 \) are immediate, and yield the desired bounds on \( \sqrt{3} \). Hence \( 4301 < \frac{A}{23} < 4302 \), so that \( N \geqslant 4302 \).

### Matching upper bound.
It remains to exhibit a covering by 4302 strips. To this end consider a net of \(\mathcal{T}\) in the form of a \( 60^\circ \)-parallelogram \( P \) with side-lengths \( a \) and \( 2a \) (area \( A \)); explicitly, this is the standard “straight” chain of the four triangular faces, which unfolds without overlap as such a parallelogram. (The internal edges of the net become the loci of permitted bends.) It will be enough to cover \( P \) itself by 4302 rectangles of dimensions \( 1 \times 23 \) contained in \( P \).

Let \( H = a \sqrt{3} \) denote the altitude of an equilateral triangle of side \( 2a \), and write \( b = \frac{H}{2} = \frac{a \sqrt{3}}{2} \) for the height of \( P \). (From the estimates \( 413 < a \sqrt{3} < 414 \) already recorded above, one has \( 206.5 < b < 207 \).) Within \( P \) one may inscribe an axis-aligned rectangle \( R \) of dimensions \( 371 \times 184 \). (To see that this fits, note that the maximal width of an axis-aligned rectangle of height 184 in \( P \) is \( 2a - \frac{184}{\sqrt{3}} \). The bounds \( 371 < 2a - \frac{184}{\sqrt{3}} < 372 \) follow on squaring from the comparisons \( \bigl( \frac{321}{184} \bigr)^2 > 3 > \bigl( \frac{318}{184} \bigr)^2 \), which are immediate upon computing \( 321^2 = 103\,041 \) and \( 3 \cdot 184^2 = 101\,568 \), resp. \( 318^2 = 101\,124 \).) Since \( 184 = 8 \cdot 23 \), the rectangle \( R \) may be tiled exactly by \( 8 \cdot 371 = 2968 \) non-overlapping copies of the \( 1 \times 23 \) rectangle (oriented with the side of length 23 parallel to the side of length 184).

The residual region \( P \setminus R \) has area \( A - 371 \cdot 184 \). Expanding \( 371 \cdot 184 = 68\,264 \) and using \( 23 \cdot 2968 = 68\,264 \), the residual area is precisely \( A - 23 \cdot 2968 \). Thus the residual area divided by 23 is \( \frac{A}{23} - 2968 \). From the earlier expansion \( \frac{A}{23} = \bigl( 2484 - \frac{11}{23} \bigr) \sqrt{3} \) we obtain \( \frac{A}{23} - 2968 = 2484 \sqrt{3} - 2968 - \frac{11}{23} \sqrt{3} \). The estimates already used for \( \sqrt{3} \) ensure that this quantity lies strictly between 1333 and 1334. In particular, the residual region has area strictly less than \( 1334 \cdot 23 \). 

Moreover, the residual region consists of a (closed) top band of \( P \) of height \( b - 184 \), together with two lateral polygonal regions of combined area exactly \( 107 \cdot 184 \). The top band, having height strictly less than 23, may be covered by 478 strips of dimensions \( 1 \times 23 \) oriented with the long side transverse to the band (each such strip covering the full transverse width available in the band while overhanging slightly into \( R \), as permitted). Separately, each lateral region admits a covering by rectangles of dimensions \( 1 \times 23 \) in which the side of length 23 runs parallel to the height-184 direction; since this height is an exact multiple of 23, and the combined lateral area is exactly \( 107 \cdot 184 \), these regions may be covered by precisely \( 107 \cdot 8 = 856 \) strips. The total number of strips used on the residual region is therefore \( 478 + 856 = 1334 \).

Combining with the 2968 strips used on \( R \), we obtain a covering of the whole of \( P \) (hence of \(\mathcal{T}\)) by \( 2968 + 1334 = 4302 \) strips, as desired.

### Conclusion.
The matching bounds yield \( N = 4302 \).

Final answer: \( 4302 \)
